translationRepairs: Lady Ruan Xiurong bore Emperor Yuan (Xiaojing) of the Shizu line;
Lady Ruan Xiurong bore Emperor Yuan (Xiao Yi) of the Shizu line;

s0004 阮脩容生世祖孝元皇帝 names the temple and posthumous titles only; the parenthetical Xiaojing invents a wrong personal name, while Xiao Yi matches the idiomatic and the historical given name used elsewhere for Emperor Yuan.
Lady Ding Chonghua bore Prince Yo of Shaoling (Xiao Lun);
Lady Ding Chonghua bore Prince Xie of Shaoling (Xiao Lun);
s0007 邵陵攜王綸 uses the posthumous title 攜, read Xie (xié); Yo is not a valid reading, so Prince Xie of Shaoling is the correct repair.
Lady Ding Chonghua bore Prince Yo of Shaoling (Lun);
Lady Ding Chonghua bore Prince Xie of Shaoling (Lun);
The literal of s0007 repeats the same mistranscription of 攜 as Yo; Xie is the accurate English for that posthumous title.

He was soon recalled by edict, but Jia Le and three hundred seventy others went to the capital and submitted a memorial listing fifteen exceptional deeds of Ji and asking that he remain in office. The emperor granted their request with a gracious edict and promoted him to General of the North Central Commandant.

He was soon recalled by edict, but Jia Le of the Bureau of the People and three hundred seventy others went to the capital and submitted a memorial listing fifteen exceptional deeds of Ji and asking that he remain in office. The emperor granted their request with a gracious edict and promoted him to General of the North Central Commandant.
s0017 民曹嘉樂 explicitly ties Jia Le to the Bureau of the People; the idiomatic omission drops source information already kept in the literal.

He was only ten days old when Prince Jian died. By three he could speak. When he saw palace women being sent away, weeping as they parted, Yili asked why. Someone said, "These were Prince Jian's women. Now that mourning is over, they are leaving."

He was only a hundred days old when Prince Jian died. By three he could speak. When he saw palace women being sent away, weeping as they parted, Yili asked why. Someone said, "These were Prince Jian's women. Now that mourning is over, they are leaving."
s0055 生十旬而簡王薨 means he had lived ten xun (one hundred days) when Prince Jian died; ten days misreads 旬 as day rather than a ten-day span.

Born at ten days, when Prince Jian died, by three he could speak. Seeing palace women being dispersed, weeping and seeing one another off, Yili asked the reason. Someone said, "These are the palace women of Prince Jian. When mourning is finished they will leave."

When he had lived a hundred days, Prince Jian died; by three he could speak. Seeing palace women being dispersed, weeping and seeing one another off, Yili asked the reason. Someone said, "These are the palace women of Prince Jian. When mourning is finished they will leave."
The literal likewise misreads 十旬 as ten days; the proposed wording restores the hundred-day interval before Prince Jian's death.
Two days into the journey, Hou Jing sent Dong Shaoxian to seize Guangling. Shaoxian pursued Huili and captured him.
Two days into the journey, Hou Jing sent Dong Shaoxian to seize Guangling. Shaoxian then pursued Huili, and Yili was captured.
In s0064 the journey subject is Yili (行二日…因爲所獲); s0065 has Shaoxian guarding him so he cannot see his brothers and then addressing his sister, so the captive is Yili, not Huili.
After two days on the road, it happened that Hou Jing sent Dong Shaoxian to seize Guangling. He then pursued Huili and was captured.
After two days on the road, it happened that Hou Jing sent Dong Shaoxian to seize Guangling. Shaoxian then pursued Huili, and Yili was captured.
The literal's passive was-captured is ambiguous; with s0065 showing Yili under Shaoxian's guard, naming Yili as the captive is required.
In the second year of Zhongdatong he died in the province at age forty-four.
In the second year of Zhong Datong he died in the province at age forty-four.
s0091 中大同二年 is the Zhong Datong era, distinct from 中大通 (Zhongdatong); collapsing the spacing wrongly identifies the wrong reign title.
Prince Yo of Shaoling, Xiao Lun, styled Shitiao, was Emperor Wu's sixth son.
Prince Xie of Shaoling, Xiao Lun, styled Shitiao, was Emperor Wu's sixth son.
s0094 邵陵攜王綸 again uses posthumous 攜; Yo is invalid and Xie is the correct English form.
Prince Yo of Shaoling, Lun, styled Shitiao, was the sixth son of Gaozu.
Prince Xie of Shaoling, Lun, styled Shitiao, was the sixth son of Gaozu.
The literal of s0094 repeats Yo for 攜; Xie correctly renders the posthumous name.
In the first year of Datong his title was restored; soon afterward he was additionally made General of Trustworthy Might, with adjutants and clerks appointed.
In the first year of Datong (AD 527) his title was restored; soon afterward he was additionally made General of Trustworthy Might, with adjutants and clerks appointed.
s0102 is 大通元年 (AD 527), not 大同 (AD 535 in this chapter); the proposed Chinese parenthetical is disallowed in English fields, so disambiguate by year instead.
In the first year of Zhong Datong he became Intendant of Danyang.
In the first year of Zhongdatong he became Intendant of Danyang.
s0103 中大通元年 is Zhongdatong, not Zhong Datong (中大同); the spaced form wrongly names the other era.

In 541 he was sent out with imperial credentials as area commander over E, Ding, Huo, and Si provinces, as General Who Pacifies the West and regional inspector of Ezhou, then transferred to General Who Secures the Vanguard and intendant of Danyang.

In 541 he was sent out with imperial credentials as area commander over Ying, Ding, Huo, and Si provinces, as General Who Pacifies the West and regional inspector of Yingzhou, then transferred to General Who Secures the Vanguard and intendant of Danyang.
s0110 郢定霍司…郢州刺史 uses 郢, conventionally Ying/Yingzhou; E/Ezhou would be 鄂 and is a place-name error.

In the seventh year he went out as bearer of the staff of authority, Area Commander of military affairs in the four provinces of E, Ding, Huo, and Si, General Who Pacifies the West, and Regional Inspector of Ezhou; he was transferred to General Who Secures the Vanguard and Intendant of Danyang.

In the seventh year he went out as bearer of the staff of authority, Area Commander of military affairs in the four provinces of Ying, Ding, Huo, and Si, General Who Pacifies the West, and Regional Inspector of Yingzhou; he was transferred to General Who Secures the Vanguard and Intendant of Danyang.
The literal repeats E/Ezhou for 郢; Ying/Yingzhou is the accurate rendering of that province name.
yet my younger brother's instruction did not relent; hence he raised troops to punish him.
yet my younger brother's admonitions also failed to make him reform; hence he raised troops to punish him.
s0142 弟教亦不悛 means the admonished party did not reform (悛), not that the brother's instruction failed to relent; the proposed sense matches the Chinese and the idiomatic.
True, a father's grievance demands brief satisfaction—but what of the nation's wrong, still unrequited?
True, a son's grievance may demand momentary satisfaction—but what of the nation's wrong, still unrequited?
s0151 子憾 is a son's grievance; father's grievance invents the wrong kinship role against the Chinese and the idiomatic.
Hou Jing was then prolonging a borrowed respite and deferring execution—the trust increased my cries of rage; I had nowhere to stand or dwell.
Hou Jing was then prolonging a borrowed respite and deferring execution—indeed this only deepened my cries of rage; I had nowhere to stand or dwell.
In s0182 信增號憤 the adverb 信 means indeed/truly intensifying the rage, not 'trust'; the proposed reading matches that sense.
Today every heart looks with eager hope to the people's sovereign. If you persist as with the Xi River affair, the times will be nearly lost.
Today every heart looks with eager hope only to grain, the people's heaven. If you persist as with the Xi River affair, the times will be nearly lost.
s0184 唯在民天, with grain discussed in s0183, uses the stock sense of grain as the people's heaven, not a sovereign; the repair restores that meaning.
The people pitied him and erected a shrine in his honor. Later Emperor Yuan posthumously titled him Yo.
The people pitied him and erected a shrine in his honor. Later Emperor Yuan posthumously titled him Xie.
s0208 追諡曰攜 awards the posthumous name 攜 (Xie); Yo is not a valid reading.
The common people pitied him and built a shrine for him. Later Emperor Yuan posthumously gave him the title Yo.
The common people pitied him and built a shrine for him. Later Emperor Yuan posthumously gave him the title Xie.
The literal likewise has Yo for 攜; Xie correctly renders the posthumous title granted by Emperor Yuan.
An edict summoned Que as General of the South Central Commandant and regional inspector of Guangzhou, with an added fief of two thousand households.
An edict summoned Que as General of the Southern Gentlemen and regional inspector of Guangzhou, with an added fief of two thousand households.
s0225 南中郎將 is the Southern Gentlemen General (南 + 中郎將), not a 'South Central Commandant' that misreads 中 as central.
An edict then summoned Que as General of the South Central Commandant and Regional Inspector of Guangzhou, with an added fief of two thousand households.
An edict then summoned Que as General of the Southern Gentlemen and Regional Inspector of Guangzhou, with an added fief of two thousand households.
The literal repeats the same misparse of 南中郎將; General of the Southern Gentlemen is the accurate office title.
Que would not budge. Prince Yo flew into a rage and told Zhao Bochao, "Bochao, cut him down for me and bring his head to the court."
Que would not budge. Prince Xie flew into a rage and told Zhao Bochao, "Qiaozhou, cut him down for me and bring his head to the court."
譙州 is the Qiaozhou address, so Bochao→Qiaozhou is right; but the same sentence's 攜王 must be Prince Xie, not Yo, so the proposed after is still incomplete.
Que's resolve was still firm. Prince Yo was greatly angered and said to Zhao Bochao, "Bochao, cut him down for me and bring his head to the court."
Que's resolve was still firm. Prince Xie was greatly angered and said to Zhao Bochao, "Qiaozhou, cut him down for me and bring his head to the court."
The vocative 譙州 correctly becomes Qiaozhou, yet 攜王 in the same unit still needs Xie rather than Yo; revise the full literal accordingly.
